Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Aerospace Dynamics Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up can be found by pressing the star key followed by one on your touchtone phone. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Global Aerospace Dynamics' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are John Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; Mike Thompson, Chief Operating Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Technology Officer; David Patel, Chief Strategy Officer; and Karen Lopez, Chief Marketing Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied.

John Harlan:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning. Global Aerospace Dynamics delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across fighter, missile, unmanned systems, and space domains. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. These programs represent the backbone of our $28.7 billion backlog, up 12% year-over-year, and continue to drive our projected mid-teens EPS growth through FY2026. We've made significant strides in development, production ramp-ups, and milestone achievements despite persistent supply chain headwinds, including titanium shortages from Ukraine-related disruptions and labor inflation averaging 6-8% in our key facilities.

Let's start with our Next Generation Air Dominance family of systems, where GAD leads the digital engineering and propulsion integrator role in partnership with Lockheed Martin and GE Aerospace. In Q3, we achieved a major milestone with the Critical Design Review completion for the adaptive cycle engine demonstrator, advancing its Technology Readiness Level from 6 to 8. This positions us for engine ground testing at Edwards AFB in Q1 2025, on track for first flight integration by 2027. Production-wise, our Low-Rate Initial Production Lot 1 contract with the USAF, valued at $2.1 billion, is 85% complete, with initial engine deliveries ramping to 12 units per month by year-end—up from 8 in Q2. Bookings here totaled $850 million in the quarter, bolstered by incremental funding from the FY2024 NDAA. Strategically, NGAD's open architecture and AI-driven mission systems are key differentiators, enabling rapid upgrades against peer competitors like China's J-20. We're also pursuing Collaborative Combat Aircraft synergies, with our SkyForge drone selected for Phase 2 prototyping.

Shifting to hypersonic programs, our Stand-Off Hypersonic Glide Vehicle under the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon program hit a pivotal milestone last month: successful end-to-end flight test from Cape Canaveral, achieving Mach 12+ speeds over a 1,800 km range with 95% telemetry recovery. This marks our third consecutive success, de-risking transition to LRIP Lot 2, a $1.4 billion award shared with Northrop Grumman. Production at our Huntsville facility is scaling from 4 all-up rounds in Q3 to 15 in Q4, with yield rates improving to 92% on boost-glide components amid RF plasma heating challenges. Revenue recognition accelerated 25% quarter-over-quarter to $420 million, driven by 70% fixed-price progress payments. Regionally, we're in advanced FMS discussions with Australia under AUKUS Pillar II, targeting a $900 million IDIQ for Pacific deterrence. Insights here underscore the urgency of hypersonics—Russia's Kinzhal and China's DF-17 deployments have compressed our timelines, prompting a 15% R&D reinvestment to counter maneuverable reentry vehicles.

On the unmanned and ISR front, our MQ-Next program, successor to the RQ-4 Global Hawk lineage in collaboration with General Atomics, passed Initial Operational Test & Evaluation with the USAF, achieving 98% mission reliability over 2,500 flight hours. Deliveries under the $3.2 billion MSA for 28 Group 5 UAS platforms reached 65% complete, with six aircraft handed over in Q3—two months ahead of schedule thanks to automated composite layup tech reducing airframe build time by 30%. Backlog funding from European partners, including a $650 million order from the UK MoD for maritime surveillance variants, reflects NATO's pivot to attritable swarms amid Baltic tensions. We're trending toward Full-Rate Production Decision in Q2 2025, with unit costs down 18% to $145 million through digital twin simulations.

In space systems, our Resilient Missile Warning satellite constellation for the Space Development Agency Tranche 2 hit full operational capability for the first 8 satellites, delivering 4K resolution IR imagery with less than 1ms latency via optical inter-satellite links. Q3 milestones included on-orbit checkout and integration with NRO's proliferated architecture, unlocking $1.1 billion in milestone payments—our largest quarterly space booking to date. Production at our Palo Alto cleanroom is at 22 satellites per year, up 40% YoY, though GEO launch delays with SpaceX have shifted two ULA Vulcan missions to Q1 2025. Strategically, we're capitalizing on the $18 billion SDA budget surge, with bids into Tranche 3 for HBTSS follow-ons. Regional commentary: Middle East allies like the UAE are accelerating $500 million in C4ISR buys to counter Houthi drone threats, diversifying our revenue 15% outside the US DoD.

Finally, a quick note on commercial aero offsets—our LEAP-X engine aftermarket for Boeing 737 MAX programs contributed $280 million in Q3, with MRO utilization at 92% capacity amid post-pandemic travel rebound. This hedges our 72% defense revenue mix.

Overall, these programs reflect disciplined execution: program margins expanded 150 basis points to 12.8%, with EAC adjustments under 2% variance. Supply chain resilience remains our focus—strategic stockpiling and dual-sourcing have mitigated 80% of inflation risks. Looking forward, we expect $4.2 billion in new awards by year-end, positioning GAD for 10-12% organic growth amid DoD's $850 billion topline and export tailwinds from the $100 billion+ global A&D market.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our NGAD program and its potential to fuel our future growth. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily.

Sarah Jenkins:
Thank you, John. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $17.2 billion, representing an 8% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $6.80. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $5.1 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at consolidated revenues of $65.2-66.5 billion, segment operating profit of $7.9-8.1 billion implying 12.1-12.2% margins, and EPS of $27.50-28.00. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 12.1%, operating income of $2.1 billion, and free cash flow of $2.8 billion year-to-date, up 15% year-over-year, fueled by strong execution on our fixed-price development contracts for the NGAD program and sustained F-35 sustainment revenues, which hit $1.2 billion in the quarter alone. Liquidity headroom exceeds $10 billion including our undrawn revolver, with net debt to EBITDA at a prudent 1.8x.

Our capital allocation philosophy is straightforward and shareholder-friendly: prioritize high-return organic investments, then return excess capital via dividends and share repurchases, and opportunistically pursue bolt-on acquisitions to enhance our technological edge. This is baked into our Investor Relations Committee playbook, stress-tested against scenarios like DoD budget sequestration risks or supply chain disruptions from legacy titanium sourcing out of Ukraine.

On dividends, we're proud to have increased our quarterly dividend by 12% to $0.65 per share, payable next month, marking our 18th consecutive annual hike. This brings our trailing 12-month yield to 2.4%, competitive with peers like Lockheed Martin at 2.7% and Northrop Grumman at 1.8%, but with a superior payout ratio of 45% of adjusted net income—well below our 60% target ceiling. This reflects confidence in our $12-14 billion multi-year FCF outlook, driven by a $185 billion backlog, 85% of which is funded and 40% international via Foreign Military Sales. Regionally, we're seeing tailwinds from NATO's 2% GDP pledge adherence; European sales jumped 22% YoY on Patriot missile co-production ramps and Eurofighter Typhoon upgrades. In Asia-Pacific, escalating tensions around the Taiwan Strait have accelerated IDIQ awards for our AN/APG-85 AESA radar family, adding $800 million to the pipeline. These secular trends—global defense spending projected at 3.5% CAGR through 2028 per SIPRI—de-risk our dividend sustainability.

On share repurchases, we've been aggressive, repurchasing $1.7 billion in shares YTD at an average price of $285, retiring 6.2 million shares or 2.1% of our float. This follows our expanded $4 billion authorization in February, with $2.3 billion remaining as of quarter-end. Our buyback yield now stands at 3.1% trailing 12 months, outpacing Boeing's sporadic activity and aligning with Raytheon's steady cadence. Why now? Our forward P/E of 16.5x trades at a 20% discount to the A&D sector average of 20.7x, per FactSet, despite our ROIC expanding to 14.2% from 12.8% last year—driven by margin expansion to 12.5% on commercial aerostructures for the 777X program. We've layered in algorithmic trading blocks during dips tied to U.S. government shutdown fears, opportunistically targeting 10-15% of daily volume. Strategically, this accretes EPS by $1.25 for FY24, supporting our 8-10% organic growth target while hedging inflation pressures on labor and composites.

For acquisitions, M&A is our growth accelerator, focused on adjacencies in hypersonics, directed energy, and uncrewed systems—areas where DoD's $145 billion FY25 budget request signals 25%+ uplift. We've deployed $650 million YTD, headlined by our August close of SkyForge Innovations for $425 million in an all-cash deal. SkyForge brings proprietary Glide Breaker-derived hypersonic kill vehicle tech, integrating seamlessly with our HAWC test bed and boosting our Joint All-Domain Technologies Center pipeline. Synergies? $45 million annualized run-rate by EOY25, primarily from G&A overlaps and cross-selling to our GhostWorks autonomy division. Regionally, this positions us for AUKUS Pillar II opportunities, where we've already secured $200 million in concept studies for hypersonic boost-glide vehicles.

We're also advancing two tuck-ins: a $150 million bid for a European C-UAS firm to counter Houthi-style drone swarms in the Red Sea corridor, and exploratory talks for Israeli gallium nitride RF tech to enhance our SPY-6 radar variants amid Middle East FMS surges up 18% YoY. Deal criteria are rigorous: targets must deliver 15%+ IRR, less than 3x EV/EBITDA multiples, and cultural fit with our 95,000-strong workforce. We've avoided mega-mergers like the aborted Aerojet Rocketdyne-LMT deal, opting for $500M-$1B bites that preserve our investment-grade A- rating from S&P.

We've allocated 25% of FCF to capex—$1.1 billion YTD—for facility modernization at our Fort Worth F-35 final assembly line and digital twin initiatives slashing NGAD prototyping costs by 30%. Debt paydown remains opportunistic; we refinanced $2 billion in 5.25% notes at 4.1% last quarter, saving $25 million annually. Risks? Supply chain snarls persist—RTX's PW8000 engine delays rippled into our commercial side—but our 98% on-time delivery rate mitigates this. Geopolitically, Ukraine aid replenishments and Indo-Pacific pivots sustain demand, with our space segment poised for NASA's $25 billion Artemis bucket.

This strategy—40% returns to shareholders, 30% organic reinvestment, 20% M&A, 10% balance sheet fortification—delivers total shareholder return north of 12% annualized over five years, outpacing the S&P A&D index by 300 basis points.

Structured into four core segments—Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control, Rotary and Mission Systems, and Space Systems—this quarter's results show Aeronautics at $6.1 billion, up 12% YoY from 152 F-35 LRIP Lot 17 deliveries; Missiles and Fire Control at $4.8 billion, +15% on JASSM-ER and PAC-3 MSE; Rotary and Mission Systems at $4.2 billion, flat but offset by CH-53K deliveries; and Space at $2.1 billion, +9% on GPS IIIF and SDA Tranche 2.

For full-year 2024, Aeronautics guides to $23.5-24.0 billion, 10-12% growth, 11.5-12.0% margins, assuming 580 F-35 deliveries and NGAD ramps; MFC to $18.0-18.5 billion, 14-16% growth, 16.0-16.5% margins on PrSM and Glide Phase Interceptor; RMS to $15.8-16.2 billion, 2-5% growth, 10.5-11.0% margins with FLRAA prototypes; Space to $7.9-8.2 billion, 10-13% growth, 11.0-11.5% margins on PWSA. Cash from operations $7.0-7.5 billion. For 2025, mid-teens EPS growth as defense topline hits $55+ billion amid 5%+ U.S. DoD topline growth and $100B+ FMS pipeline.

Diving into revenue drivers, our Defense segment at 62% grew 12% on fixed-wing and missiles, Commercial Aviation at 28% up 5% on 737 MAX stabilization, Space at 10% surging 22%. Tailwinds from FY2024 NDAA $886 billion, F-35 $1.1 billion revenues, hypersonic IDIQ $2.4 billion, international up 20% on NATO and Asia-Pacific. Commercial green shoots from 737/787 ramps and Vulcan missions. R&D at $1.2 billion improved execution 15%.

Headwinds shaved 200 bps: supply chain on titanium/rare earths deferring $150 million, labor turnover delaying CH-53K, inflation at 6.2% PPI, commercial softness, ITAR delays. Mitigated via $500 million inventory, Supplier Resilience Program, AeroAcademy upskilling, MRO pivot up 14%.

On margins, consolidated SAOM 11.8%, up 120 bps YoY. Defense 13.2%, Shadowhawk LRIP 14.5%; Space 10.4%, Orion 11.2%; Commercial 9.1%, Titan 10.8%. Favorable CVs like +$450 million on fighters, MBSE on 85% programs, titanium hedging. Targeting 12.5% FY25.

Key guidance assumptions: FY24 NDAA $886 billion, 95% disbursements, NATO 2%, inflation 2.5-3%; program ramps like 156 F-35s, NGAD $1.2 billion; margins from FPIF mix, cost-outs; regions U.S./Indo-Pacific 55%, Europe 20%; investments in hypersonics, MBSE. Risks: CRs ±1% topline, inflation 50 bps hit.

Geopolitics: Global spend $2.24 trillion up 6.8%, to $2.4 trillion. Europe 15.4% to €295 billion on Ukraine 2M rounds; Indo-Pacific on China A2/AD, PDI $9.1 billion; Middle East on Houthis, GCC $140 billion. Budget shift to peers, hypersonics +25%.

Mike Thompson:
Thank you, Sarah. Operationally, we have seen significant improvements in our supply chain management, allowing us to increase production rates on key programs like F-35 Lot 17 and hypersonic rounds. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies, including additive manufacturing and AI predictive maintenance, to improve efficiency and reduce costs by 20-30% on airframe builds. Specifically, our Fort Worth and Huntsville facilities achieved 92% capacity utilization, with digital twin simulations cutting NGAD prototyping time and on-time delivery at 98%. We've upskilled 2,000 machinists via AeroAcademy, targeting 95% fill rates, and dual-sourced 70% of critical avionics with partners like Honeywell.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Mike. On the technology front, we're making significant strides in our next-generation propulsion systems, including adaptive cycle engines for NGAD and hypersonic boost-glide vehicles. We anticipate these advancements will give us a competitive edge, with TRL 8 on demonstrators and 3D-printed TPS cutting costs 40%. More specifically, AI/ML for swarming tactics in MQ-Next, GaN RF for SPY-6, and MBSE accelerating EMD phases by 12 months across 80% of programs. Our GhostWorks autonomy division integrates SkyForge tech for CCA drone teaming, positioning us for Replicator initiatives.

David Patel:
Thank you, Lisa. From a strategic perspective, we are actively evaluating potential acquisitions like the European C-UAS tuck-in to complement our portfolio and expand market reach into counter-drone for Red Sea ops. We are also focused on developing new business models, such as performance-based logistics for F-35 sustainment and proliferated LEO for SDA, to capture emerging opportunities in autonomy and space resilience. For instance, AUKUS Pillar II concept studies and PWSA bids target 25% non-U.S. revenues by 2027, leveraging NATO 2030 and Pacific Deterrence.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Josh Klein with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Josh Klein:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the updates to key programs like NGAD and hypersonics, especially milestones and production ramps?

John Harlan:
Certainly, Josh. As I detailed earlier, NGAD hit CDR for the adaptive cycle engine, TRL 8 now, with LRIP Lot 1 85% complete and ramping to 12 engines monthly. Hypersonics nailed Mach 12+ flight test, third success, scaling Huntsville to 15 rounds Q4 at 92% yields. These de-risk $4.2 billion new awards expected year-end, amid strong DoD and FMS demand.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Tran with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Tran:
Hi, I'm curious about revenue drivers, headwinds, and your capital deployment, particularly buybacks and M&A?

Sarah Jenkins:
Emily, drivers include F-35 $1.1 billion up 18%, hypersonics $950 million +25%, international +20% on NATO/Asia. Headwinds like titanium shortages deferred $150 million, but mitigated with dual-sourcing. On capital, $1.7 billion repurchases YTD at $285 average, 3.1% yield; dividend to $0.65/share; $650 million M&A like SkyForge $425 million for hypersonic synergies, $45 million run-rate.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Raj Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Raj Patel:
Regarding the geopolitical factors and guidance assumptions, how are you factoring in Ukraine, Indo-Pacific, and DoD budgets?

Lisa Chen:
Raj, geopolitics drives $2.24 trillion global spend, Europe +15% on Ukraine munitions burn, Indo-Pacific PDI $9.1 billion for NGAD/CCAs. Guidance assumes FY24 NDAA $886 billion, 95% pacing, NATO 2%, hypersonics ramps at 98% delivery. Sensitivities like CRs ±1%, but $125 billion backlog at 4.3x book-to-bill buffers.

John Harlan:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call. A replay and transcript will be available on our investor relations website.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
